steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a generalizable neural BRDF representation that can estimate materials from sparse, unstructured samples and compress measured BRDFs. Cover the problem, why analytic fitting and per-material neural fields fall short, how generalizable neural fields help, our framework, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. BRDFs and what we propose
2. Limits of analytic / PCA fitting and measured data
3. Neural fields for BRDFs and their limits
4. Generalizable Neural Fields (GNFs)
5. Our framework and its efficiency
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. BRDFs
- realistic rendering of intricate materials depends on describing light-surface interaction
- conventionally: modeling + reconstruction of 4D Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF), relates incident and outgoing light intensities for a material
- we propose: generalizable BRDF representation model; estimate BRDFs of new materials from highly sparse, unstructured point-based samples; compress dense values into very small latent embeddings

2. Prior fitting
- estimate free parameters of analytic BRDFs or principal components, from images or reflectance measurements
- oversimplified models -> inaccurate for real materials, less realism
- nonlinear optimization fitting: unstable, expensive, local minima
- measured BRDFs: errors from equipment limitations

3. Neural fields
- deep learning: complex continuous signals (images, surfaces, volumes, materials) with a Neural Field = network mapping coordinates to sampled values; compact
- popular for continuous BRDFs in recent works
- but: regression loss, overfit to single material; dense sampling, heavy compute; no generalization to new materials

4. GNFs
- learn generalized mapping (deterministic or probabilistic) from sampled signals to full neural field, like supervised learning
- condition neural field on latent embedding of samples
- mechanisms: concatenated latent vectors, hypernetworks, attention-based set latent representations
- at inference: reconstruct full signal even from highly sparse, unstructured samples

5. Our framework
- estimation of unseen materials from sparse unstructured samples + compression of measured BRDFs into low-dimensional latent space
- MLP neural field backbone; hyper-network for conditioning; set encoder: arbitrary number of measurements from arbitrary directions -> compact latent embedding
- hyper-network nonlinear interpolation -> material editing and blending across sample sizes
- efficient, no per-material overfitting; state-of-the-art accuracy for sample size below 4000 (Figure 4)

6. Contributions
- generalizability/adaptability: varying sample sizes and appearances; unseen materials from sparse sampling; compact representation, beats prior state-of-the-art compression (Table 2)
- realism/accuracy: 20 test materials, 40 to 4000 samples; better appearance modeling + color preservation (at least 2dB PSNR, 1 in Delta E)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In computer graphics and vision, getting realistic renderings for intricate surface materials depends on describing accurately how light interacts with the surfaces. Conventionally this is done by modeling and reconstructing a 4D Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF), which quantifies the relationship between the incident and the outgoing light intensities for a specific material. In this work we propose a new generalizable BRDF representation model. It can estimate the BRDFs of new materials from highly sparse and unstructured point-based samples, and it can compress densely sampled values into very small latent embeddings.

There is prior work that tries to tackle similar tasks by estimating the free parameters of analytic BRDF functions, or the principal components of BRDF functions, from images or reflectance measurements. But the models of the complex BRDF function are oversimplified, and this leads to inaccuracies when predicting real materials, so the renderings are less realistic. Also, fitting through nonlinear optimization is unstable by nature, computationally expensive and prone to local minima, and this hinders reconstructing material appearance accurately. On top of that, measured BRDFs of real-world materials can have errors because of equipment limitations, which makes the fitting even more complex.

Recent advances in deep learning have made it possible to represent complex continuous signals (e.g. images, surfaces, volumes, materials, etc.) accurately using a Neural Field, i.e. a neural network that maps coordinate inputs to sampled values, and this without compromising how compact the model is. Because of this, neural fields have become very popular for representing continuous BRDFs in recent works. However, to reconstruct a neural field representation for BRDFs you typically have to train the network with a regression loss function so that it overfits to a single material. This needs dense sampling and a lot of computational resources, and it cannot generalize to new materials.

- GNFs: learn generalized mapping (deterministic or probabilistic) from sampled signals to full neural field, like supervised learning; condition on latent embedding of samples; concatenated latent vectors, hypernetworks, attention-based set latents; full signal at inference even from highly sparse, unstructured samples
- our framework: estimation of unseen materials + compression into low-dimensional latent space; MLP backbone, hyper-network conditioning, set encoder (arbitrary number of measurements, arbitrary directions -> compact latent)
- hyper-network nonlinear interpolation -> material editing/blending across sample sizes
- efficient, no per-material overfitting; state-of-the-art accuracy below 4000 samples (Figure 4)
- contributions: generalizability/adaptability (unseen materials, compact representation, beats prior compression method, Table 2); realism/accuracy (20 test materials, 40 to 4000 samples, at least 2dB PSNR and 1 in Delta E)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In computer graphics and vision, getting realistic renderings for intricate surface materials depends on describing accurately how light interacts with the surfaces. Conventionally this is done by modeling and reconstructing a 4D Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF), which quantifies the relationship between the incident and the outgoing light intensities for a specific material. In this work we propose a new generalizable BRDF representation model. It can estimate the BRDFs of new materials from highly sparse and unstructured point-based samples, and it can compress densely sampled values into very small latent embeddings.

There is prior work that tries to tackle similar tasks by estimating the free parameters of analytic BRDF functions, or the principal components of BRDF functions, from images or reflectance measurements. But the models of the complex BRDF function are oversimplified, and this leads to inaccuracies when predicting real materials, so the renderings are less realistic. Also, fitting through nonlinear optimization is unstable by nature, computationally expensive and prone to local minima, and this hinders reconstructing material appearance accurately. On top of that, measured BRDFs of real-world materials can have errors because of equipment limitations, which makes the fitting even more complex.

Recent advances in deep learning have made it possible to represent complex continuous signals (e.g. images, surfaces, volumes, materials, etc.) accurately using a Neural Field, i.e. a neural network that maps coordinate inputs to sampled values, and this without compromising how compact the model is. Because of this, neural fields have become very popular for representing continuous BRDFs in recent works. However, to reconstruct a neural field representation for BRDFs you typically have to train the network with a regression loss function so that it overfits to a single material. This needs dense sampling and a lot of computational resources, and it cannot generalize to new materials.

More recently Generalizable Neural Fields (GNFs) have come up as a promising solution to these challenges. GNFs do not overfit to individual signals, instead they are designed to learn a generalized mapping, which can be deterministic or probabilistic, between the sampled signals and their full neural field representations, similar to supervised learning. The key strategy in GNFs is to condition the neural fields on a latent embedding of the signal samples. Popular ways of conditioning are concatenated latent vectors, hypernetworks, and attention-based set latent representations. Once the conditional neural field is learned properly, the full signal can be reconstructed at inference time, even with highly sparse and unstructured samples.

Inspired by GNFs, we propose a new framework for generalizable neural BRDF representation. It is for both estimating unseen materials from sparse and unstructured samples and compressing measured BRDFs into a low-dimensional latent space. In the framework we use a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) model as the neural field backbone for the BRDF representation, a hyper-network for the conditioning, and a set encoder that maps an arbitrary number of reflectance measurements from arbitrary directions to a compact latent embedding for conditional BRDF generation. The hyper-network also has a built-in nonlinear interpolation capability, which gives robust and adaptable material editing and blending across various sample sizes.

Different from previous work, our BRDF reconstruction is very efficient and does not need extensive training to overfit individual materials, and it still keeps state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy for sample size below 4000; see Figure 4.

So in summary we offer a new solution for the challenging task of generalizable BRDF modelling, with these key contributions:

- Generalizability and Adaptability: Our method is robust and adaptable across varying sample sizes and appearances, so it is very effective for estimating the BRDFs of unseen materials from highly sparse and unstructured sampling. The adaptability also extends to highly compact representation of BRDFs, where overall it outperforms the prior state-of-the-art compression method; see Table 2.

- Realism and Accuracy: Our extensive evaluation shows the superior performance of our approach when reconstructing the BRDFs of 20 test materials from a limited number of samples, from 40 to 4000. It outperforms prior methods in appearance modeling and color preservation (by at least 2dB in peak-signal-to-noise ratio and 1 in Delta E).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In computer graphics and vision, achieving realistic renderings of intricate surface materials depends on accurately describing the interaction of light with the surfaces. This is conventionally done by modeling and reconstructing a 4D Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF), which quantifies the relationship between the incident and outgoing light intensities for a specific material. In this work, we propose a novel generalizable BRDF representation model that can estimate the BRDFs of new materials from highly sparse and unstructured point-based samples and compress densely sampled values into very small latent embeddings.

While prior work has tackled similar tasks by estimating the free parameters of analytic BRDF functions or the principal components of BRDF functions from images or reflectance measurements, these oversimplified models of the complex BRDF function lead to inaccuracies when predicting real materials, diminishing the realism of renderings [1]. Moreover, fitting through nonlinear optimization is inherently unstable, computationally expensive, and prone to local minima, which hinders accurate reconstruction of material appearance [2,3]. Measured BRDFs of real-world materials can also contain errors due to equipment limitations, adding to the complexity of the fitting process [4].

Recent advances in deep learning have enabled accurate representation of complex continuous signals (e.g. images, surfaces, volumes, materials, etc.) using a Neural Field [5,6,7], i.e. a neural network mapping coordinate inputs to sampled values, without compromising model compactness. Consequently, neural fields have become popular for representing continuous BRDFs in recent works [8,7]. However, reconstructing a neural field representation for BRDFs typically requires training the network with a regression loss function to overfit to a single material, which demands dense sampling and extensive computational resources and cannot generalize to new materials.

More recently, Generalizable Neural Fields [9] (GNFs) have emerged as a promising solution to these challenges. Rather than overfitting to individual signals, GNFs learn a generalized mapping, either deterministic or probabilistic, between sampled signals and their full neural field representations, in a fashion similar to supervised learning. The key strategy of GNFs is conditioning the neural fields with a latent embedding of the signal samples. Popular conditioning mechanisms include concatenated latent vectors [10], hypernetworks [11], and attention-based set latent representations [12]. Once the conditional neural field is properly learned, the full signal can be reconstructed at inference time, even from highly sparse and unstructured samples.

Inspired by GNFs, we propose a novel framework for generalizable neural BRDF representation, both for estimating unseen materials from sparse and unstructured samples and for compressing measured BRDFs into a low-dimensional latent space. In this framework, we use a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) model as the neural field backbone for BRDF representation, a hyper-network for conditioning, and a set encoder that maps an arbitrary number of reflectance measurements from arbitrary directions to a compact latent embedding for conditional BRDF generation. The built-in nonlinear interpolation capability of the hyper-network also enables robust and adaptable material editing and blending across various sample sizes.

Unlike previous work, our BRDF reconstruction is highly efficient, with no need for extensive training to overfit individual materials, while maintaining state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy for sample size below 4000; see Figure 4.

In summary, we offer a novel solution for the challenging task of generalizable BRDF modelling with the following key contributions:

- Generalizability and Adaptability: Our method is robust and adaptable across varying sample sizes and appearances, making it highly effective for estimating the BRDFs of unseen materials from highly sparse and unstructured sampling. This adaptability also extends to highly compact representation of BRDFs, overall outperforming the prior state-of-the-art compression method; see Table 2.

- Realism and Accuracy: Our extensive evaluation demonstrates the superior performance of our approach in reconstructing the BRDFs of 20 test materials from a limited number of samples, ranging from 40 to 4000, outperforming prior methods in appearance modeling and color preservation (by at least 2dB in peak-signal-to-noise ratio and 1 in Delta E).
